summary: Specializing in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology, Lokesh Chandra earned his master's from the University of the Punjab and his Ph.D. at Utrecht University under Jan Gonda. He served as Secretary (~1957–1963) and Director (~1963–2022) of the International Academy of Indian Culture.
Longlian was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Fazun in 1939 and under the traditional teacher Nenghai Shi from circa 1941 to 1967.

Specializing in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Iranian and Central Asian studies, Sander studied under Ernst Waldschmidt (~1962–1967). She served as Curator at the Museum of Asian Art in 1987 and as a lecturer at the Free University of Berlin in 1994.

Focusing on Japanology, Buddhist studies, and religious studies, Meeks earned her BA from Columbia and her PhD from Princeton under Jacqueline I. Stone. She became an Assistant Professor of Religious Studies at the University of Southern California in 2004.

Dewaraja specialized in history, archaeology, and Buddhist studies. After studying at the University of Ceylon and the University of London, she served as Associate Professor of History at the University of Peradeniya (~1961–1978) and held posts at the University of Colombo and St Anne's College.

Ledderose worked in Sinology, Buddhist studies, and history and archaeology, completing his Habilitation at the University of Cologne after studying at Heidelberg, Bonn, Princeton, Harvard, and Tokyo. He was Professor at Heidelberg University (~1976–2010) and President of the Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft (1978–1990).

Falkenhausen, a scholar of Sinology, history, and archaeology, studied at Bonn, Peking, Harvard (MA, PhD), and Kyoto. He held appointments at UC Riverside and joined UCLA in 1993, becoming Full Professor and later Associate Director (2004–2011).

Casartelli worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies and linguistics, studying at Ushaw College, the University of London, and KU Leuven under Charles-Joseph de Harlez de Deulin. He served as Professor of Zend and Pehlevi at KU Leuven and taught at Manchester.

Specializing in linguistics and Indology, Deroy studied at KU Leuven and the University of Paris. He built his career at the University of Liège, serving successively as chef de travaux (1956), Assistant (1960), Professeur associé (1965), and Professeur ordinaire (1972).

Dubeux worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies and linguistics, studying under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy and Antoine-Léonard Chézy. He served at the Royal Danish Library, as Professor of Turkish at INALCO (1848–1849), and as Professor of Hebrew at Collège de France (1857–1862).

Dumont worked in Indology and religious studies, studying at the EPHE, Institut d'ethnologie, and University of Paris under Marcel Mauss, Walther Schubring, and Pierre Meile. He taught at Oxford (1951–1955) before serving as Directeur d'Études at EPHE and EHESS.

Specializing in history, archaeology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies, Dupree earned his BA from Harvard University (~1946–1949). He later held posts at Pennsylvania State University, Princeton, the United States Military Academy, Duke University, and UNC Chapel Hill.

Duvau was a linguistics scholar who studied at the Faculty of Arts of Paris, the École Pratique des Hautes Études, and the University of Leipzig, learning under Ferdinand de Saussure (~1883–1887). He held a post at the École française de Rome (1887–1888).

Finot studied at EPHE under Sylvain Lévi and specialized in Indology, history, archaeology, and Buddhist studies. He was Director of the École française d'Extrême-Orient (1899–1904), taught at EPHE (1895–1930), and served as Professor of Indochinese History and Philology at Collège de France (1920–1930).
Frédéric was a scholar of history, archaeology, Japanology, and Indology who completed his studies at the Sorbonne and the École Pratique des Hautes Études.
Gabaude specialized in Buddhist studies and religious studies, holding a long-term post at the École française d'Extrême-Orient from circa 1980 to 2007.

A scholar of history and archaeology, Gernet studied at the École Normale Supérieure (~1902–1905). He subsequently held posts at the University of Algiers (~1921–1948) and the École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1948–1961).

Gray specialized in Iranian and Central Asian studies, linguistics, and Indology, earning his degrees from Princeton and Columbia under A. V. Williams Jackson. He held posts at Princeton, Nebraska-Lincoln, and served as Professor of Comparative Linguistics at Columbia (1926–1944).

Hambis specialized in Iranian and Central Asian studies, Sinology, and history, studying under Paul Pelliot and at EPHE. He served as Directeur d'études at EPHE (1952) and Professor of Central Asian History and Civilizations at Collège de France (1965–1977).
A linguistics scholar, Havet studied at EPHE under Michel Bréal, Abel Bergaigne, and Gaston Paris (~1868–1872). He served as Professor of Latin Philology at the Collège de France from 1885 to 1925.
